common_name: Williford's Anthurium (Narrow-Leaf Miniature Bird's Nest Anthurium)

planting.note: Divide offsets from the base of the rosette once they have several roots of their own, and pot into a small, shallow container with a fine, fast-draining aroid mix; this Peruvian miniature stays compact and is well suited to terrariums, vivariums, and small-pot windowsill culture rather than open floor space.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light with no direct sun in a fine-textured, fast-draining aroid mix; Anthurium willifordii is a diminutive terrestrial to epiphytic species from Peruvian Amazon cloud forest that forms a tight rosette of narrow, glossy, dark green, strap-shaped leaves rarely more than a few inches long, making it one of the smallest species regularly grown in cultivation. Its miniature bird's-nest habit and slow, clumping growth suit it to terrarium and vivarium culture, where the constant high humidity (60% or more) it needs is easier to maintain than in open room air. Keep the mix evenly moist but never waterlogged, and avoid letting the small root mass dry out completely, since this species has little reserve capacity compared to larger, thicker-leaved Anthurium relatives. Offsets form slowly at the base and can be divided once independently rooted. All parts toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted offsets in a well-drained, humus-rich aroid mix in a shaded, humid spot; this Central American species is widely grown commercially as cut foliage and as a durable, easy-care houseplant thanks to its tolerance of average home humidity better than many velvet-leaf relatives.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate light in a well-drained, humus-rich aroid mix; native from Nicaragua and Costa Rica south into Panama and Colombia, Anthurium friedrichsthalii forms an upright clump of long, narrow, pendent, strap-shaped leaves with a leathery texture and glossy dark green surface, giving the plant an airy, grass-like or willowy appearance distinct from the broad-leaved bird's-nest and velvet-leaf Anthurium types. Its slender, tail-like spadix and small greenish-white spathe are inconspicuous, and the species is grown almost entirely for its narrow, arching foliage, which is harvested commercially as cut greenery in tropical floriculture and valued by houseplant growers for its tolerance of average indoor humidity. Water when the top inch of mix dries out, and provide steady warmth above 60F; the plant is more forgiving of fluctuating humidity than most collector-grade Anthurium species. All parts toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Pot divisions into a chunky, well-aerated aroid mix and grow in warm, shaded, humid conditions; native to the Andean foothill cloud forests around Salgar in Antioquia, Colombia, this species prefers cooler night temperatures than many lowland velvet-leaf Anthurium relatives.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix with high humidity; Anthurium salgarense is a Colombian foothill-forest species named for the Antioquia municipality of Salgar, prized in the collector trade for its glossy, dark green, ovate-cordate leaves and contrasting reddish-bronze new growth and cataphylls. The high-gloss leaf surface and compact, clumping habit set it apart from the matte, velvety texture of many related collector Anthuriums, making it useful for growers who want foliage contrast within a mixed aroid display. Keep the mix evenly moist but never soggy, provide consistent warmth with some night cooling to mimic its mid-elevation cloud-forest origin, and avoid direct sun, which will scorch the glossy leaf surface. All parts toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Pot in a chunky, bark-based aroid mix and keep in warm, shaded, high-humidity conditions; the deeply wrinkled leaf surface of this Ecuadorian and Colombian foothill species holds moisture and debris more readily than smooth-leaved relatives, so periodic gentle rinsing helps prevent fungal spotting.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a chunky, well-aerated, bark-based aroid mix with consistently high humidity above 65%; Anthurium rugulosum is a collector-grade species from Andean foothill forest in Ecuador and Colombia, named for the distinctly rugulose (finely wrinkled and puckered) surface texture of its broad, dark blackish-green, velvety leaves. The corrugated leaf surface, set off by pale, deeply impressed primary veins, gives the foliage a sculptural, almost quilted appearance similar in spirit to other prized velvet anthuriums, though the wrinkling is finer and more irregular than the bold bullate panels of species like A. dressleri. Keep the mix evenly moist without waterlogging, avoid cold drafts and temperatures below 60F, and provide steady bright shade rather than any direct sun, which will bleach and scorch the velvety leaf surface. A slower-growing species best suited to experienced collectors with reliable humidity control. All parts toxic if ingested.

common_name: Obake Anthurium (Pinwheel Flamingo Flower, Hawaiian Twist-Spathe Anthurium)

planting.note: Divide rooted basal offsets and pot into a well-drained, humus-rich aroid mix; Obake-type anthuriums are Hawaiian-bred novelty selections grown for their unusually shaped, multicolored spathes rather than a distinct wild species, so plants are propagated vegetatively to preserve the twisted, pinwheel form.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light with humus-rich, fast-draining aroid mix and steady warmth and humidity; 'Obake' (Japanese for "shapeshifter" or "ghost") is a trade name used for a group of Hawaiian-bred Anthurium andraeanum selections prized for their unusual, twisted, multi-lobed spathes that flare into an irregular pinwheel shape rather than the smooth heart-shaped spathe of standard flamingo flowers. Obake-type spathes typically show striking two-tone or shaded color combinations, commonly green blending into red, pink, orange, or white, with the color pattern shifting as each flower matures, and the glossy heart-shaped leaves are similar to standard A. andraeanum. Feed lightly during the growing season, keep the mix evenly moist without waterlogging, and provide bright indirect light; too little light reduces flowering and spathe color intensity, while direct sun scorches both leaves and spathes. Popular as a novelty cut flower and specimen houseplant among collectors who value unusual bloom form over the classic glossy heart shape. All parts toxic if ingested.
